assessment:
Cast a black tutor at this table and three seats decide you are digging for the infinite. You are almost never digging for the infinite.

The loop assembles in 4.8% of your games on natural draws and 24.3% when a wish goes into it — so carry the ticket and never steer for it. Your default wish is the missing half of the go-wide kill: a converter that turns every token entry into damage at three seats, or the multiplier beside it.

That kill is why the tutors exist. It is online by turn six in 41.7% of games off your natural draws and 57.7% once a tutor is spent on it — sixteen points of your kill rate live in these three cards, so spend them on the plan and stop saving them for something cleverer.

Your commander is not the early game. He lands on a mean turn 6.6 and is down by turn six in 52.1% of games, so the wishes have to win the first five turns without him — and they can, because a converter lands on a mean turn 2.8.

Three wishes, all blank cheques. Demonic Tutor is two mana, any card, to hand — the workhorse. Diabolic Intent is the same contract with a creature sacrificed on top, and eminence prints that currency: a 1/1 from the command zone on every Vampire spell you cast. Vampiric Tutor is one mana at instant speed for any card on TOP of your library plus two life — it costs your next draw, so it is the end-step wish, cast when the table's mana is spent and cashed the turn it arrives.

One structural fact governs every loop wish. Bloodthirsty Conqueror is half of both verified infinites — stacks 004 and 006 — so when you do buy the loop, fetch toward the half you already hold and keep two doors open instead of one. He is also a 5/5 creature, which hands the table an instant-speed removal window. Count their open mana first, then spend the wish happily.

And one cost governs the flashiest closer. Bloodletter of Aclazotz is the only triple-black cast in the 99, in your thinnest colour — 27 black sources against a 36-source yardstick — so never fetch him onto a board that cannot pay {B}{B}{B} on schedule.

tutors.notes: Two mana, any card, straight to hand — the only wish that hands you a spell you cast the same turn. Mean available mana is 4.006 on turn four, so plan it as Tutor plus a two-drop on four and Tutor plus a three-drop on five; anything dearer means you are buying next turn, and you should say that out loud before you cast it. Never ask it for your best card. Ask which missing piece turns the board you already have — 2.9 bodies by turn four — into damage at three seats.

targets.scenario: Turn four. Edgar is in the command zone, you have three bodies and a token doubler down, and nothing on the battlefield converts an entry into damage. Player 2 is the durdle seat on four lands; Player 3 has a 4/4 and is looking at you.
targets.why: Take the cheapest door into your actual plan and take it now. Two for the Tutor and two for Tremors is the whole of turn four at 4.006 mean mana — cast both and pass with the layer live. From then on every eminence token is one damage to each seat, no combat step, no blocker. The converter layer is down by turn six in only 62.6% of games on natural draws, so a third of your games ask you to go and get it. Go and get it.

citations.quote: Your cards should do something to all three seats or win the game

targets.scenario: The turn after a board wipe resolved. You kept two lands and a Vampire in hand, Edgar is back in the command zone, and the table thinks you are out of the game for three turns.
targets.why: Rebuild into cards, not just bodies. Skullclamp costs one to cast and one to equip, and every 1/1 that dies under it draws you two — so each Vampire spell you cast from here mints an eminence token that is itself two cards on demand. Your draw engine is online by turn six in only 62.2% of games unassisted; after a wipe is exactly when you are on the wrong side of that number, and this is the cheapest engine in the 99 to deploy off two lands.

citations.quote: redeploy worst-first, keeping the best threat in hand for their second sweeper

targets.scenario: Turn six or later. Anointed Procession and Mondrak, Glory Dominus are both on the battlefield, you hold a two-mana Vampire, and all three opponents are above 20 life. Nobody is attacking you because your board is 1/1s.
targets.why: Close it — the arithmetic is already on the record. Stack 008 ran one two-mana Vampire through the 1-to-2-to-4 eminence doubling as five Purphoros triggers: ten damage to each opponent off a single cheap cast. Hold the two-drop until Purphoros lands, then cast it and hand the whole table a Lava Axe. Deploy him into the sweeper seat's held mana without flinching: he is indestructible, and at this deck's devotion he is usually not even a creature.

citations.quote: reach must scale (each-opponent drains, commander damage, damage doublers)

targets.scenario: The wish nobody sees coming. The blue seat has held two untapped Islands every turn and countered the last two spells anyone tried to resolve. You have a hand of Vampires and no way to make one stick.
targets.why: Fetching a land looks like a waste until you name what it buys. Choose Vampire and every Vampire creature spell you cast can no longer be countered — their whole held plan goes blank for the rest of the game. It also fixes your short colour: black sits at 27 sources against a 36-source yardstick. One rule so it never surprises you: Cavern's coloured mana pays only for creature spells, so tap it for colourless — or tap another land — when you want Vito's lifelink activation.

citations.quote: ask which of the opponent's likely cards your permanent invalidates

tutors.notes: One mana at instant speed, any card, on TOP — plus two life and your next draw. That shape dictates the timing: cast it at the end step right before your untap, when the table's mana and attention are spent, and only when you will cast the card the turn it arrives. A Vampiric cast three turns early is a card spent arranging a draw you then draw into removal range. Pay the two life without blinking — Sanctum Seeker and the lifegain halves hand it straight back.

targets.scenario: Opponent 3's end step, turn four. You have a doubler and five bodies but no converter, three untapped lands, and your untap is next. Player 2 just tapped out for a planeswalker.
targets.why: The go-wide kill is online by turn six in 41.7% of your games on natural draws and 57.7% with a wish spent on it — this is the wish, at the moment the table cannot answer it. Roastmaster is the converter on a body: every later entry is one damage to each seat, and he triggers the other converters on his own way in. One mana at their end step, cast him on your turn with mana to spare.

citations.quote: prefer committing at the end step before your own turn so the table's chances to respond are spent

targets.scenario: The sweeper seat has held five mana across two turns and is visibly waiting. You have seven Vampires, the table knows the wipe is coming, and your hand is lands.
targets.why: Make the wipe cost them the game instead of costing you yours. With Celebrant down, every creature you lose drains each opponent for one and pays you one — seven deaths is seven off each seat while you rebuild from the command zone. Prefer him over Blood Artist when the whole table matters: Artist drains one target player per death, Celebrant hits everyone. Fetch at their end step, cast him for two, and stop being afraid of the wipe.

citations.quote: buy resilience instead of restraint where you can

targets.scenario: Sanctum Seeker and six other Vampires are on your board, untapped, and your attack is next turn. Two opponents are at 14 and 16. You can pay {B}{B}{B} plus one.
targets.why: This is the closing fetch, and the maths is verified: stack 003 resolves a seven-Vampire attack with Bloodletter and Sanctum Seeker as 14 life off each opponent on attack declaration alone — before a single point of combat damage. Both life totals in this scenario are inside that number. The rule attached: he is the only triple-black cast in the 99, so confirm the {B}{B}{B} is actually there before the wish, not after.

targets.scenario: The wish nobody sees coming. Player 2's Ghostly Prison-style tax has shut off your combat, your hand has no answer, and the rest of the table is shrugging because it does not tax them.
targets.why: You draw an answer to a noncreature permanent by turn six in only 42.8% of games — more than half the time you hold none, and that is what this wish is for. Gift is the deck's true catch-all: it destroys ANY permanent, lands included, at instant speed. The 3/3 Elephant you hand back is a blocker against the wrong seat and nothing against a board that drains on entry and death. Fetch it, hold it, and spend it on the piece taxing YOU — let the bystanders answer everything else.

citations.quote: hold single-target removal until the threat is pointed at you

tutors.notes: Two mana and a creature sacrificed as an additional cost — and eminence prints that currency, minting a 1/1 from the command zone on every Vampire spell you cast. Spend a token, never a lord. Two upgrades to look for before you cast it: with Cordial Vampire out the sacrifice puts a +1/+1 counter on every Vampire you control, so sequence Intent after Cordial and the cost becomes an anthem; with Blood Artist or Cruel Celebrant out, the cost drains on its way to the graveyard. The one time Intent is wrong is the one time it looks right: when your only body is your only blocker, that body is not spare — that is Demonic Tutor's job.

targets.scenario: Turn five. You have four bodies including a spare token, every seat is developing, and your 1/1s are bouncing off 3/3 blockers. No converter on the battlefield.
targets.why: Take the payoff that repays the sacrifice twice. One damage to each opponent on every entry, plus a permanent +1/+1 to your whole board — the token you spent comes straight back as a point of power on everything you own, and your swarm stops bouncing. Three mana on top of the two-mana Intent against 4.729 mean mana on turn five: that is the whole turn, and it is the right whole turn.

targets.scenario: Turn five or six. Seven Vampires on your board, one of them a spare token, and your hand is empty. The table is leaving you alone because you look topdecked.
targets.why: Refill from the width you already built. Champion draws you a card per Vampire on entry — and he counts himself plus the eminence token his own cast mints, so sacrifice the spare token to Intent and six on board still resolves as eight cards drawn. The draw engine assembles in 73.4% of games and this is how you land on the right side of it when the natural draw missed. Double black: check the 27 sources can pay {3}{B}{B} this turn, not next. If his seat is already spent, Pact of the Serpent is the same effect for three mana.

targets.scenario: Impact Tremors is on the battlefield and undisturbed, you have five bodies and a Vampire in hand, and the table has spent its removal on each other. All three opponents are above 25.
targets.why: Double every future entry, on a 4/4 body. Stack 002 verified the doubling as one event and order-independent — one eminence trigger becomes two tokens, two doublers make four — so stop sequencing cleverly and just resolve him. The go-wide kill goes 41.7% to 57.7% by turn six with a wish, and this fetch is what that second number is made of. Bank the neat part: his indestructible activation eats two spare tokens, the exact currency Intent taught you to farm.

targets.scenario: The wish nobody sees coming. Player 3 has resolved a Rhystic Study-style engine and is pulling ahead of the whole table. Your board is fine; your hand has Vampires and no answer.
targets.why: Exile any nonland permanent at instant speed, and pay the three life without thinking in a deck whose drains and lifelink refill it. You draw an answer to a noncreature permanent in 52.9% of games — half the time it is not coming on its own, so the moment an engine or stax piece resolves against you, this is the wish. Fetch it and HOLD it: let another seat spend theirs first, and spend yours on the piece actually beating you.

citations.quote: hold removal until the threat is pointed at you

gaps: The goldfish prices all three tutors as unrestricted wildcards to hand. Vampiric Tutor's top-of-library lag and two-life cost, and Diabolic Intent's sacrifice cost, are not modelled — so the assisted figures are a ceiling on those two thirds of the tutor suite, and the coaching above prices the costs in prose instead.
Nothing simulates opposing interaction: every fetch-versus-hold call against held removal or counterspells here is coaching judgment on top of measured assembly rates, not measurement.

There is no graveyard answer in the 99 to fetch — confirmed at the oracle level in the diagnosis — so against a reanimator seat these tutors buy speed, never an answer. A tutor cannot buy a class the deck does not hold.
